query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailoring the eutectic lamellar microstructure by a controlled thermo‐mechanical processing route (e.g., cold rolling followed by optimized annealing) in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 will simultaneously enhance room-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy characterized by coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies with multiple internal boundaries that serve as sites for microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored thermo-mechanical processing regime (such as a defined cold rolling reduction followed by an annealing step) to refine the lamellar colony size and improve interface quality.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; processing parameters must be optimized to refine the microstructure without inducing phase coarsening or excessive embrittlement.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine duplex lamellar microstructure featuring refined colony size and enhanced interface density, which increases the number of crack-arresting barriers.
generation.mechanism: Refining the lamellar colonies increases the density and quality of phase boundaries, which can arrest and deflect microcracks during deformation while enhancing strain hardening, leading to improved strength and ductility relative to the as-cast microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified as-cast baseline, the processed alloy will exhibit higher yield/fracture strength along with increased room-temperature tensile ductility.
generation.baseline: The as-cast lamellar structure of AlCoCrFeNi2.1, which demonstrates a tradeoff where increased strength comes with limited ductility due to microcrack initiation at coarse internal boundaries.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only if the dual-phase (e.g., soft FCC and hard B2) nature of the eutectic alloy is maintained; over-refinement or improper processing could lead to embrittlement. The hypothesis is confined to eutectic high-entropy alloys similar in composition and processing history to AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative enhancement in strength and ductility as a result of the tailored processing is uncertain and will require systematic experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples: one set as-cast (baseline) and one set subjected to the tailored thermo-mechanical processing (e.g., controlled cold rolling with a specified reduction followed by annealing). Conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both sets while characterizing the microstructure (lamellar spacing, colony refinement, and interface quality) using SEM/TEM.
measurements: Tensile strength (proof stress and fracture stress)
Microstructural characterization (lamellar spacing, colony size, interface density)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermo-mechanically processed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility (or if ductility deteriorates due to embrittlement) compared to the as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs.
